nodes.name: PIMAC (2-user Gaussian MAC interfering with a P2P link)
nodes.statement: A Gaussian 2-user multiple access channel (MAC) and a Gaussian point-to-point (P2P) channel use the same medium for their communication. They interfere with each other as shown in Figure \ref{pIMAC}. We call the resulting setup the PIMAC, whose received signals can be written as \begin{align} Y_1&=X_1+X_2+h_{31}X_3+Z_1,\\ Y_2&=h_{12}X_1+h_{22}X_2+X_3+Z_2, \end{align} where $h_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}$ denotes the channel coefficient from transmitter $i\in\{1,2,3\}$ to receiver $j\in\{1,2\}$, $X_i$ is the transmit symbol of transmitter $i$ and $Z_j$ is an additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) with $Z_j\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$. Transmitter $i$ has power constraint $P_i$ so that $\mathbb{E}[X_i^2]\leq P_i$.
nodes.statement_short: The PIMAC: a Gaussian 2-user MAC and a Gaussian P2P link sharing one medium, with outputs $Y_1=X_1+X_2+h_{31}X_3+Z_1$ and $Y_2=h_{12}X_1+h_{22}X_2+X_3+Z_2$.
nodes.genus: A Gaussian 2-user multiple access channel (MAC) and a Gaussian point-to-point (P2P) channel
differentia: use the same medium for their communication

nodes.name: Encoding and decoding functions of the PIMAC
nodes.statement: The transmitters encode their messages $m_i$ chosen independently from $\mathcal{M}_i=\{1,\dots,2^{nR_i}\}$ into a codeword of length $n$ symbols $X_i^n\in\mathbb{R}^n$ $$X_i^n=(X_{i,1},\dots,X_{i,n})$$ using encoding functions $f_i$. Receiver 1 decodes $m_1$ and $m_2$ by using a decoding function $g_1$, i.e. $(\hat{m}_1,\hat{m}_2)=g(Y_1^n)$, and receiver 2 decodes $m_3$ by using a decoding function $g_2$, i.e. $\hat{m}_3=g_2(Y_2^n)$. A decoding error $E_i$ occurs if $m_i\neq\hat{m}_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Messages $m_i$ from $\mathcal{M}_i=\{1,\dots,2^{nR_i}\}$ are encoded into length-$n$ codewords; receiver 1 decodes $(m_1,m_2)$, receiver 2 decodes $m_3$.

nodes.name: $(n,2^{nR_1},2^{nR_2},2^{nR_3})$ code and average probability of error
nodes.statement: An $(n,2^{nR_1},2^{nR_2},2^{nR_3})$ code for the PIMAC consists of encoding functions, decoding functions, and message sets, and induces an average probability of decoding error given by \begin{align} P^{(n)}=\frac{1}{2^{nR_\Sigma}}\sum_{\vec{m}\in\mathcal{M}_1\times\mathcal{M}_2\times\mathcal{M}_3}P\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^3E_i\right), \end{align} where $R_\Sigma=\sum_{i=1}^3R_i$ and $\vec{m}=(m_1,m_2,m_3)$.
nodes.statement_short: A code is a triple of message sets with encoders and decoders; its average error probability $P^{(n)}$ is the union of the three decoding-error events.
nodes.genus: encoding functions, decoding functions, and message sets

nodes.name: Achievable rate tuple, capacity region $\mathcal{C}$ and sum capacity $C_\Sigma$
nodes.statement: A rate tuple $(R_1,R_2,R_3)$ is achievable if there exists a sequence of $(n,2^{nR_1},2^{nR_2},2^{nR_3})$ codes such that $P^{(n)}]\to0$ as $n\to\infty$. The closure of the set of all achievable rates is the capacity region of the PIMAC denoted $\mathcal{C}$, and the sum capacity is the highest achievable sum-rate \begin{align} C_\Sigma=\max_{(R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}}R_\Sigma. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: A rate tuple is achievable if some code sequence drives $P^{(n)}\to0$; $\mathcal{C}$ is the closure of achievable rates and $C_\Sigma$ its largest sum-rate.
nodes.definiendum: the capacity region of the PIMAC denoted $\mathcal{C}$
nodes.genus: The closure of the set of all achievable rates

nodes.name: $M(\mathcal{S},j)$ and its capacity region $\mathcal{C}^M(\mathcal{S},j)$
nodes.statement: We denote a multiple access channel MAC from transmitters $i\in\mathcal{S}\subseteq\{1,2,3\}$ to receiver $j\in\{1,2\}$ with AWGN with variance $1$ by $M(\mathcal{S},j)$ and its corresponding capacity region by $\mathcal{C}^M(\mathcal{S},j)$. This region is given by \begin{equation*} \mathcal{C}^M(\mathcal{S},j)=\left\{ \begin{array}{l} R_i\geq0\ \ \forall i \in \mathcal{S}: \forall \mathcal{T}\subseteq\mathcal{S}\\ \sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}R_i\leq\frac{1}{2}\log\left(1+\sum_{i\in\mathcal{T}}h_{ij}^2P_i\right) \end{array} \right\}. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Notation: $M(\mathcal{S},j)$ is the unit-noise AWGN MAC from the transmitters in $\mathcal{S}$ to receiver $j$, with the usual subset sum-rate region $\mathcal{C}^M(\mathcal{S},j)$.
nodes.genus: a multiple access channel MAC from transmitters $i\in\mathcal{S}\subseteq\{1,2,3\}$ to receiver $j\in\{1,2\}$

nodes.name: Outer bound on the capacity region of the PIMAC
nodes.statement: The capacity region of the PIMAC is outer bounded by $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$, $$\mathcal{C}\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{C}}$$ where \begin{align*} \overline{\mathcal{C}}=\left\{ \begin{array}{lr} (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathbb{R}_+^3:&\\ R_3\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_3)&\\ (R_1,R_2)\in\mathcal{C}^M(\{1,2\},1)&\\ (R_1,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,3\},2)& \text{ if } h_{12}^2\geq1\\ (R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{2,3\},2)& \text{ if } h_{22}^2\geq1\\ (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},1)& \text{ if } h_{31}^2\geq1 \end{array}\right\}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{C}$ is contained in the intersection of the interference-free P2P and MAC bounds with the MAC regions that become valid whenever the corresponding cross gain exceeds one.
assumptions: $h_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}$ denotes the channel coefficient from transmitter $i\in\{1,2,3\}$ to receiver $j\in\{1,2\}$
Transmitter $i$ has power constraint $P_i$ so that $\mathbb{E}[X_i^2]\leq P_i$
conclusions: The capacity region of the PIMAC is outer bounded by $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$, $$\mathcal{C}\subseteq\overline{\mathcal{C}}$$

nodes.name: Inner bound on the capacity region of the PIMAC
nodes.statement: The capacity region of the PIMAC is inner bounded by $\underline{\mathcal{C}}$, $$\underline{\mathcal{C}}\subseteq\mathcal{C}$$ where \begin{align} \underline{\mathcal{C}}=\left\{ \begin{array}{l} (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathbb{R}_+^3:\\ (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},1)\\ (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},2) \end{array}\right\}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Letting both receivers decode all three messages achieves the intersection of the two 3-user MAC regions $\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},1)$ and $\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},2)$.
assumptions: $h_{ij}\in\mathbb{R}$ denotes the channel coefficient from transmitter $i\in\{1,2,3\}$ to receiver $j\in\{1,2\}$
Transmitter $i$ has power constraint $P_i$ so that $\mathbb{E}[X_i^2]\leq P_i$
conclusions: The capacity region of the PIMAC is inner bounded by $\underline{\mathcal{C}}$, $$\underline{\mathcal{C}}\subseteq\mathcal{C}$$

nodes.name: Capacity region of the PIMAC with strong interference
nodes.statement: If the PIMAC satisfies the following conditions \begin{align} h_{12}^2,h_{22}^2,h_{31}^2&\geq1\\ h_{12}^2P_1+h_{22}^2P_2+P_3&\geq P_1+P_2+h_{31}^2P_3, \end{align} then the outer bound $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$ and the inner bound $\underline{\mathcal{C}}$ coincide and hence, the capacity region of the PIMAC is \begin{align} \mathcal{C}=\overline{\mathcal{C}}=\underline{\mathcal{C}}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Under strong interference plus a power-ordering condition the outer and inner bounds coincide, so the capacity region is exactly their common value.
conclusions: then the outer bound $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$ and the inner bound $\underline{\mathcal{C}}$ coincide and hence, the capacity region of the PIMAC is

nodes.name: Reduced outer bound for the PIMAC with strong interference
nodes.statement: According to Lemma \ref{pSILemma}, any achievable rate tuple $(R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathbb{R}_+^3$ for PIMAC with strong interference must satisfy \begin{align} (R_1,R_3)&\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,3\},2)\\ (R_2,R_3)&\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{2,3\},2)\\ (R_1,R_2,R_3)&\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},1). \end{align} where the remaining bounds $R_3\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_3)$ and $(R_1,R_2)\in\mathcal{C}^M(\{1,2\},1)$ were removed because they are already included in (\ref{SIB3})-(\ref{SIB5}).
nodes.statement_short: Under strong interference only the three MAC constraints (SIB3)-(SIB5) remain; the P2P and 2-user MAC bounds are implied by them.
assumptions: Let us now consider special cases of the PIMAC with strong interference $h_{12}^2,h_{22}^2,h_{31}^2\geq1$

nodes.name: Capacity region under very strong interference from transmitter 1 to receiver 2
nodes.statement: If the PIMAC satisfies (\ref{VSI12-1})-(\ref{VSI12-3}) then its capacity region is \begin{align} \mathcal{C}=\left\{ \begin{array}{l} (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathbb{R}_+^3:\\ (R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{2,3\},2)\\ (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},1) \end{array}\right\}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: When the interference from transmitter 1 to receiver 2 is very strong the capacity region is the intersection of $\mathcal{C}_M(\{2,3\},2)$ and $\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},1)$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Very strong interference from transmitter 1 to receiver 2

nodes.name: Capacity region under very strong interference from transmitter 3 to receiver 1
nodes.statement: If the PIMAC satisfies (\ref{VSI31-1})-(\ref{VSI31-3}) and (\ref{VSI31-4}), then its capacity region is \begin{align} \mathcal{C}=\left\{ \begin{array}{l} (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathbb{R}_+^3:\\ (R_1,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,3\},2)\\ (R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{2,3\},2)\\ (R_1,R_2)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2\},1) \end{array}\right\}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: When the interference from transmitter 3 to receiver 1 is very strong and an extra power condition holds, the capacity region reduces to two 2-user MAC regions at receiver 2 plus the interference-free MAC region at receiver 1.
nodes.section: 4.2 Very strong interference from transmitter 3 to receiver 1

nodes.name: Capacity region of the PIMAC with very strong interference
nodes.statement: If the PIMAC satisfies (\ref{pIMAC-VSI1}) and (\ref{pIMAC-VSI2}), then its capacity region is \begin{align} \mathcal{C}=\left\{ \begin{array}{l} (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathbb{R}_+^3:\\ R_3\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_3)\\ (R_1,R_2)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2\},1) \end{array}\right\}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: With very strong interference in both directions, interference costs nothing: the interference-free MAC region and the P2P capacity are simultaneously achievable.
nodes.section: 4.3 The PIMAC with very strong interference
conclusions: then its capacity region is \begin{align} \mathcal{C}=\left\{ \begin{array}{l} (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathbb{R}_+^3:\\ R_3\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_3)\\ (R_1,R_2)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2\},1) \end{array}\right\}. \end{align}

nodes.name: Sum capacity upper bound $\overline{C}_\Sigma$ for the PIMAC
nodes.statement: The sum capacity of the PIMAC is upper bounded by $\overline{C}_\Sigma$, i.e. $$C_\Sigma\leq\overline{C}_\Sigma$$ where \begin{align} \overline{C}_\Sigma&\triangleq\min_{\substack{|\rho_1|,|\rho_2|\leq1,\\ \eta_1^2\leq1-\rho_2^2,\\ \eta_2^2\leq1-\rho_1^2}} I(X_{1G},X_{2G};Y_{1G},S_{1G})+I(X_{3G};Y_{2G},S_{2G}) \end{align} with $X_{iG}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,P_i)$, $Y_{iG}$ is the corresponding channel output when the input is $X_{iG}$ and \begin{align} S_{1G}&=h_{12}X_{1G}+h_{22}X_{2G}+\eta_1W_1\\ S_{2G}&=h_{31}X_{3G}+\eta_2W_2, \end{align} where $W_i\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ for $i\in\{1,2\}$ such that $\mathbb{E}[W_iZ_i]=\rho_i$.
nodes.statement_short: A genie-aided argument bounds the sum capacity by a minimum over the genie-noise correlations of two Gaussian mutual-information terms.
assumptions: with $X_{iG}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,P_i)$, $Y_{iG}$ is the corresponding channel output when the input is $X_{iG}$
conclusions: The sum capacity of the PIMAC is upper bounded by $\overline{C}_\Sigma$, i.e. $$C_\Sigma\leq\overline{C}_\Sigma$$

nodes.name: Sum capacity lower bound by treating interference as noise
nodes.statement: A trivial sum capacity lower bound is obtained by using Gaussian codes and treating interference as noise. The resulting lower bound is given by \begin{align} C_\Sigma\geq\underline{C}_\Sigma&=\frac{1}{2}\log\left(1+\frac{P_1+P_2}{1+h_{31}^2P_3}\right)\nonumber\\ &\quad+\frac{1}{2}\log\left(1+\frac{P_3}{1+h_{12}^2P_1+h_{22}^2P_2}\right). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Gaussian codes with interference treated as noise give the sum-rate lower bound $\underline{C}_\Sigma$.
assumptions: using Gaussian codes and treating interference as noise
conclusions: The resulting lower bound is given by \begin{align} C_\Sigma\geq\underline{C}_\Sigma&=\frac{1}{2}\log\left(1+\frac{P_1+P_2}{1+h_{31}^2P_3}\right)\nonumber\\ &\quad+\frac{1}{2}\log\left(1+\frac{P_3}{1+h_{12}^2P_1+h_{22}^2P_2}\right). \end{align}

nodes.name: Tightness of the sum capacity bounds when $h_{12}=h_{22}=h$
nodes.statement: In the special case of $h_{12}=h_{22}=h$, then the PIMAC becomes similar to a 2-user IC with transmit signals $X_1^n+X_2^n$ and $X_3^n$. In this case, the bounds $\overline{C}_\Sigma$ in Theorem (\ref{SumCapacityUpperBound}) and $\underline{C}_\Sigma$ in (\ref{CS_LB}) coincide if $|h|(1+h_{31}^2P_3)+|h_{31}|(1+h^2(P_1+P_2))\leq1$.
nodes.statement_short: For $h_{12}=h_{22}=h$ the PIMAC reduces to a 2-user IC and the sum-capacity upper and lower bounds meet under an explicit noisy-interference condition.

nodes.name: Very strong interference from transmitter 1 to receiver 2
nodes.statement: Consider a PIMAC with strong interference such that interference from transmitter 1 to receiver 2 is very strong, \begin{align} h_{12}^2&\geq1+P_3+h_{22}^2P_2\\ h_{22}^2&\geq1\\ h_{31}^2&\geq1. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Regime: $h_{12}^2\geq1+P_3+h_{22}^2P_2$ while the other two cross links are merely strong.
nodes.section: 4.1 Very strong interference from transmitter 1 to receiver 2

nodes.name: Very strong interference from transmitter 3 to receiver 1
nodes.statement: Suppose that the PIMAC has \begin{align} h_{12}^2&\geq1\\ h_{22}^2&\geq1\\ h_{31}^2&\geq1+P_1+P_2. \end{align}
nodes.section: 4.2 Very strong interference from transmitter 3 to receiver 1

nodes.name: Additional power condition for very strong interference from transmitter 3 to receiver 1
nodes.statement: If we have \begin{align} h_{12}^2P_1+h_{22}^2P_2\geq(P_1+P_2)(1+P_3), \end{align}
nodes.section: 4.2 Very strong interference from transmitter 3 to receiver 1

nodes.name: PIMAC with very strong interference
nodes.statement: Consider now the PIMAC with very strong interference such that \begin{align} h_{12}^2,h_{22}^2&\geq1+P_3\\ h_{31}^2&\geq1+P_1+P_2. \end{align}
nodes.section: 4.3 The PIMAC with very strong interference

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1 (deferred)
nodes.statement: The proof is based on arguments similar to Sato's arguments in \cite{Sato} and is given in Appendix \ref{pSILemmaProof}.
nodes.statement_short: Deferred to the appendix; follows Sato's outer-bounding argument.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1
nodes.statement: Each receiver simply decodes all messages in a MAC fashion. The achievable rates must be in the intersection of $\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},1)$ and $\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},2)$ and the statement of the theorem follows.
nodes.statement_short: Direct achievability: both receivers decode all three messages, so the rates lie in the intersection of the two MAC regions.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2 (deferred)
nodes.statement: By expanding the achievable region $\underline{\mathcal{C}}$, and using conditions (\ref{pSI1}) and (\ref{pSI2}), it can be shown that $\underline{\mathcal{C}}$ reduces to $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$ and the result follows. Details are given in Appendix \ref{pSIProof}.
nodes.statement_short: Expand the inner bound under the two conditions and check it collapses onto the outer bound; details deferred to the appendix.

nodes.name: Proof of the capacity region under very strong interference from transmitter 1 to receiver 2
nodes.statement: Since $h_{12}^2\geq1+P_3+h_{22}^2P_2\geq1+P_3$, then it can be shown that the bound (\ref{SIB3}) is redundant and can be removed. Thus the outer bound becomes \begin{align} \left\{ \begin{array}{l} (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathbb{R}_+^3:\\ (R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{2,3\},2)\\ (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},1) \end{array}\right\}. \end{align} Moreover $h_{12}^2\geq1+P_3+h_{22}^2P_2\Rightarrow$ \begin{align} \frac{1}{2}\log\left(1+\frac{h_{12}^2P_1}{1+P_3+h_{22}^2P_2}\right)\geq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_1). \end{align} This means that the second receiver can decode $X_1^n$ while treating $X_2^n$ and $X_3^n$ as noise without imposing an additional rate constraint on the achievable rates. Then by subtracting the contribution of $X_1^n$ from $Y_2^n$, and decoding $X_2^n$ and $X_3^n$ in a MAC fashion at the second receiver, the rate region $\mathcal{C}^M(\{2,3\},2)$ can be achieved. If the first receiver decodes all signals in a MAC fashion, the rate region $\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},1)$ can be achieved. Therefore we have the following theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Drop the redundant bound (SIB3) from the outer bound, then match it by decoding and stripping $X_1^n$ at receiver 2 and MAC-decoding everything at receiver 1.
nodes.section: 4.1 Very strong interference from transmitter 1 to receiver 2

nodes.name: Proof of the capacity region under very strong interference from transmitter 3 to receiver 1
nodes.statement: In this case, the rate restriction (\ref{SIB5}) can be replaced with \begin{align} (R_1,R_2)&\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2\},1), \end{align} which follows since the rate upper bounds on $R_3$, $R_1+R_3$, $R_2+R_3$, and $R_1+R_2+R_3$ are all redundant given $(R_1,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,3\},2)$ and $(R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{2,3\},2)$. Therefore, the following capacity outer bound holds \begin{align} \left\{ \begin{array}{l} (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathbb{R}_+^3:\\ (R_1,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,3\},2)\\ (R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{2,3\},2)\\ (R_1,R_2)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2\},1) \end{array}\right\}. \end{align} This outer bound can be achieved if we add one more condition on the PIMAC as we show next. If (\ref{VSI31-3}) holds then receiver 1 can decode $X_3^n$ while treating $X_1^n$ and $X_2^n$ as noise without imposing an additional rate constraint on $m_3$. This follows since (\ref{VSI31-3}) $\Rightarrow$ \begin{align} \frac{1}{2}\log\left(1+\frac{h_{31}^2P_3}{1+P_1+P_2}\right)\geq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_3). \end{align} Thus, receiver 1 can remove the contribution of $X_3^n$ from $Y_1^n$ and then decode $X_1^n$ and $X_2^n$ achieving $\mathcal{C}^M(\{1,2\},1)$. Let receiver 2 decode all signals in a MAC fashion achieving the region $(R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},2)$. If we have \begin{align} h_{12}^2P_1+h_{22}^2P_2\geq(P_1+P_2)(1+P_3), \end{align} then the bound on $R_1+R_2+R_3$ in $\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},2)$ becomes redundant and can be removed. This follows since \begin{align} &h_{12}^2P_1+h_{22}^2P_2\geq(P_1+P_2)(1+P_3)\Rightarrow\\ &\frac{1}{2}\log(1+h_{12}^2P_1+h_{22}^2P_2+P_3)\geq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_1+P_2)\nonumber\\ &\hspace{5cm}+\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_3). \end{align} Thus, under condition (\ref{VSI31-4}) and given $(R_1,R_2)\in\mathcal{C}^M(\{1,2\},1)$ we can replace $(R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},2)$ by \begin{align} (R_1,R_2)&\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2\},2)\\ (R_1,R_3)&\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,3\},2)\\ (R_2,R_3)&\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{2,3\},2). \end{align} Now, since the region $\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2\},2)$ is larger than $\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2\},1)$, we obtain the following theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Replace the redundant sum-rate constraint, then achieve the resulting region by decoding and stripping $X_3^n$ at receiver 1 and MAC-decoding at receiver 2 under the extra power condition.
nodes.section: 4.2 Very strong interference from transmitter 3 to receiver 1

nodes.name: Proof of the capacity region of the PIMAC with very strong interference
nodes.statement: In this case, interference does not reduce capacity, i.e. the capacity region of the interference free MAC $M(\{1,2\},1)$ can be achieved by $(R_1,R_2)$ and the point-to-point capacity $R_3=\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_3)$ can also be achieved. Clearly, the following outer bound holds for the PIMAC \begin{align} \left\{ \begin{array}{l} (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathbb{R}_+^3:\\ R_3\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_3)\\ (R_1,R_2)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2\},1) \end{array}\right\}. \end{align} This outer bound can be achieved under the given conditions (\ref{pIMAC-VSI1}) and (\ref{pIMAC-VSI2}) by decoding interference first at each receiver while treating the desired signal as noise, and then decoding the desired signal after removing the contribution of interference. Thus, as if interference is not present, the capacity region of the pIMAC becomes as given in the following theorem.
nodes.statement_short: The trivial interference-free outer bound is matched by decoding interference first at each receiver and subtracting it.
nodes.section: 4.3 The PIMAC with very strong interference

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 6 (deferred)
nodes.statement: We use a genie aided approach similar to \cite{AnnapureddyVeeravalli} to bound $R_1+R_2$ and $R_3$. After adding the bounds, we observe that their sum is maximized by Gaussian inputs and we obtain the upper bound. Details are given in Appendix \ref{SumCapacityUpperBoundProof}.
nodes.statement_short: Genie-aided bounding of $R_1+R_2$ and $R_3$ separately, then add and maximize over Gaussian inputs; details deferred to the appendix.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 1
nodes.statement: Clearly, for any achievable rate triple $(R_1,R_2,R_3)$, the rate $R_3$ is upper bounded by the interference free capacity of the P2P channel, and the rate couple $(R_1,R_2)$ is included in the capacity region of the interference free MAC $M(\{1,2\},1)$, i.e. \begin{align} R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_3)\\ (R_1,R_2)&\in\mathcal{C}^{M}(\{1,2\},1). \end{align} Now we derive the other bounds. A genie gives $m_2$ as additional information to the second receiver. The obtained genie aided channel has a larger capacity region than the original PIMAC and can be used to outer bound $\mathcal{C}$. Now consider a rate tuple $(R_1,R_2,R_3)$ in the capacity region of the genie aided channel. This means that the first receiver and the second receiver are able to decode $(m_1,m_2)$ and $m_3$ reliably respectively. Since the second receiver is able to decode $m_3$, and since it knows $m_2$ from the genie, then it is able to construct \begin{align} \tilde{Y}_1^n&=\frac{Y_2^n-h_{22}X_2^n-X_3^n}{h_{12}}+X_2^n+h_{31}X_3^n\nonumber\\ &=X_1^n+X_2^n+h_{31}X_3^n+\frac{1}{h_{12}}Z_2^n \end{align} If $h_{12}^2\geq1$, then $\tilde{Y}_1^n$ is a less noisy version of $Y_1^n$. So if the first receiver is able to decode $m_1$ then so does the second receiver. Thus $(R_1,R_3)$ is contained in the MAC region of $M(\{2,3\},2)$, i.e. \begin{align} (R_1,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}^{M}(\{1,3\},2) \text{ if } h_{12}^2\geq1. \end{align} Similarly, we can show that \begin{align} (R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}^{M}(\{2,3\},2) &\text{ if } h_{22}^2\geq1. \end{align} Finally, for any rate triple $(R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}$, the first receiver is able to decode $m_1$ and $m_2$ reliably. Thus, if $h_{31}^2\geq1$, receiver 1 can construct a less noisy version of $Y_2^n$ and then decode $m_3$ reliably leading to the bound \begin{align} (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}^{M}(\{1,2,3\},1) &\text{ if } h_{31}^2\geq1. \end{align} and the statement of the Lemma is proved.
nodes.statement_short: Genie-aided converse in Sato's style: give $m_2$ to receiver 2, build a less noisy output, and read off each MAC constraint.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2
nodes.statement: We can expand the achievable region $\underline{\mathcal{C}}$ to obtain the following rate constraints for the achievable region \begin{align*} R_1&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_1,h_{12}^2P_1\})\\ R_2&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_2,h_{22}^2P_2\})\\ R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_3,h_{31}^2P_3\})\\ R_1+R_2&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_1+P_2,h_{12}^2P_1+h_{22}^2P_2\})\\ R_1+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_1+h_{31}^2P_3,h_{12}^2P_1+P_3\})\\ R_2+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_2+h_{31}^2P_3,h_{22}^2P_2+P_3\})\\ R_1+R_2+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_1+P_2+h_{31}^2P_3,\\ &\hspace{3cm}h_{12}^2P_1+h_{22}^2P_2+P_3\}) \end{align*} Using conditions (\ref{pSI1}) and (\ref{pSI2}), these constraints reduce to \begin{align*} R_i&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_i),\ \forall i\in\{1,2,3\}\\ R_1+R_2&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_1+P_2)\\ R_1+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_1+h_{31}^2P_3)\\ R_1+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+h_{12}^2P_1+P_3)\\ R_2+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_2+h_{31}^2P_3)\\ R_2+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+h_{22}^2P_2+P_3)\\ R_1+R_2+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_1+P_2+h_{31}^2P_3). \end{align*} Expanding $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$ when conditions (\ref{pSI1}) and (\ref{pSI2}) hold lead to the same rate constraints. Thus, the two regions $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$ and $\underline{\mathcal{C}}$ coincide and the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Expand both regions into explicit rate constraints and check that the strong interference conditions make the two constraint lists identical.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 6
nodes.statement:
Consider the following signals  egin{align} S_1^n&=h_{12}X_1^n+h_{22}X_2^n+\eta_1W_1^n\ S_2^n&=h_{31}X_3^n+\eta_2W_2^n \end{align} where $\eta_i\in\mathbb{R}$ and $W_i^n$ is an i.i.d. sequence with $W_i\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ for $i\in\{1,2\}$ such that $\mathbb{E}[W_iZ_i]=ho_i$. A genie gives these signals as extra information to the receivers. Thus, receiver $i$ knows both $Y_i^n$ and $S_i^n$ and uses them for decoding. Using Fano's inequality, we have  egin{align} n(R_1+R_2)&\leq I(X_1^n,X_2^n;Y_1^n,S_1^n)+n\epsilon_{1n}\ nR_3&\leq I(X_3^n;Y_2^n,S_2^n)+n\epsilon_{2n} \end{align} where $\epsilon_{1n},\epsilon_{2n}	o0$ as $n	o\infty$. Using the chain rule, we can write  egin{align} n(R_1+R_2-\epsilon_{1n})&\leq I(X_1^n,X_2^n;S_1^n)+I(X_1^n,X_2^n;Y_1^n|S_1^n)
onumber\ &=h(S_1^n)-h(S_1^n|X_1^n,X_2^n)+h(Y_1^n|S_1^n)
onumber\ &\quad-h(Y_1^n|S_1^n,X_1^n,X_2^n). \end{align} Similarly  egin{align} n(R_3-\epsilon_{2n})&\leq h(S_2^n)-h(S_2^n|X_3^n)+h(Y_2^n|S_2^n)
onumber\ &\quad-h(Y_2^n|S_2^n,X_3^n). \end{align} The next step is to show that sum of the above quantities (ef{Q1}) and (ef{Q2}) are maximized when $X_i^n$ is i.i.d. Gaussian for all $i\in\{1,2,3\}$, i.e. $X_i\sim\mathcal{N}(0,P_i^*)$ where $P_i^*\leq P_i$. We will denote that Gaussian $X_i$ as $X_{iG}$ and the corresponding outputs as $Y_{iG}$ and $S_{iG}$. Since the Gaussian distribution maximizes the conditional differential entropy under a covariance constraint, we have  egin{align} h(Y_1^n|S_1^n)&\leq nh(Y_{1G}|S_{1G})\ h(Y_2^n|S_2^n)&\leq nh(Y_{2G}|S_{2G}). \end{align} Furthermore, the terms $h(S_1^n|X_1^n,X_2^n)$ and $h(S_2^n|X_3^n)$ are independent of the distribution of $X_i$. Now, we jointly maximize the difference $h(S_1^n)-h(Y_2^n|S_2^n,X_3^n)$ as follows  egin{align} &\hspace{-1cm}h(S_1^n)-h(Y_2^n|S_2^n,X_3^n)
onumber\ &=h(h_{12}X_1^n+h_{22}X_2^n+\eta_1W_1^n)
onumber\ &\quad-h(h_{12}X_1^n+h_{22}X_2^n+Z_2^n|W_2^n)\ &\stackrel{(a)}{=}h(h_{12}X_1^n+h_{22}X_2^n+\eta_1W_1^n)
onumber\ &\quad-h(h_{12}X_1^n+h_{22}X_2^n+V_2^n)\ &\stackrel{(b)}{\leq}nh(h_{12}X_{1G}+h_{22}X_{2G}+\eta_1W_1)
onumber\ &\quad-nh(h_{12}X_{1G}+h_{22}X_{2G}+V_2)\ &=nh(S_{1G})-nh(Y_{2G}|S_{2G},X_{3G},X_{4G}), \end{align} where $(a)$ follows from \cite[Lemma 6]{AnnapureddyVeeravalli} with $V_2^n$ being an i.i.d. Gaussian sequence with $V_2\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1-ho_2^2)$ and $(b)$ from the worst case noise \cite{DiggaviCover} such that $\eta_1^2\leq 1-ho_2^2$. Since $\eta_1^2\leq1-ho_2^2$, (ef{T1}) can be shown to be increasing in $P_1^*$ and $P_2^*$ and thus is maximized by $X_{iG}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,P_i)$. Similarly, if $\eta_2^2\leq1-ho_1^2$, $h(S_2^n)-h(Y_1^n|S_1^n,X_1^n,X_2^n)$ can be shown to be maximized by $X_{iG}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,P_i)$. Moreover, $h(Y_{1G}|S_{1G})$ and $h(Y_{2G}|S_{2G})$ can be shown to be increasing in $P_i^*$ and thus also maximized by $X_{iG}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,P_i)$. As a result, by letting $n	o\infty$  egin{align} &R_1+R_2+R_3
onumber\ &\quad\leq I(X_{1G},X_{2G};Y_{1G},S_{1G})+I(X_{3G};Y_{2G},S_{2G}) \end{align} with $X_{iG}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,P_i)$ and $\eta_i\leq1-ho_j^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Give the genie signals $S_i^n$ to the receivers, apply Fano and the chain rule, then show the resulting entropy differences are maximized by Gaussian inputs at full power.

nodes.name: Remove the redundant bound (SIB3)
nodes.statement: Since $h_{12}^2\geq1+P_3+h_{22}^2P_2\geq1+P_3$, then it can be shown that the bound (\ref{SIB3}) is redundant and can be removed. Thus the outer bound becomes \begin{align} \left\{ \begin{array}{l} (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathbb{R}_+^3:\\ (R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{2,3\},2)\\ (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},1) \end{array}\right\}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Show (SIB3) is implied by the other constraints and delete it from the outer bound.
nodes.section: 4.1 Very strong interference from transmitter 1 to receiver 2

nodes.name: Very strong interference implies no rate penalty for decoding $X_1^n$
nodes.statement: Moreover $h_{12}^2\geq1+P_3+h_{22}^2P_2\Rightarrow$ \begin{align} \frac{1}{2}\log\left(1+\frac{h_{12}^2P_1}{1+P_3+h_{22}^2P_2}\right)\geq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_1). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Translate the channel condition into the rate inequality that makes decoding $X_1^n$ free.
nodes.section: 4.1 Very strong interference from transmitter 1 to receiver 2

nodes.name: Achievability at receiver 2 by successive decoding
nodes.statement: This means that the second receiver can decode $X_1^n$ while treating $X_2^n$ and $X_3^n$ as noise without imposing an additional rate constraint on the achievable rates. Then by subtracting the contribution of $X_1^n$ from $Y_2^n$, and decoding $X_2^n$ and $X_3^n$ in a MAC fashion at the second receiver, the rate region $\mathcal{C}^M(\{2,3\},2)$ can be achieved.
nodes.statement_short: Receiver 2 decodes and subtracts $X_1^n$, then MAC-decodes $X_2^n,X_3^n$.
nodes.section: 4.1 Very strong interference from transmitter 1 to receiver 2

nodes.name: Achievability at receiver 1 and conclusion
nodes.statement: If the first receiver decodes all signals in a MAC fashion, the rate region $\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},1)$ can be achieved. Therefore we have the following theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Receiver 1 MAC-decodes everything, matching the reduced outer bound.
nodes.section: 4.1 Very strong interference from transmitter 1 to receiver 2

nodes.name: Replace the redundant sum-rate constraint (SIB5)
nodes.statement: In this case, the rate restriction (\ref{SIB5}) can be replaced with \begin{align} (R_1,R_2)&\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2\},1), \end{align} which follows since the rate upper bounds on $R_3$, $R_1+R_3$, $R_2+R_3$, and $R_1+R_2+R_3$ are all redundant given $(R_1,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,3\},2)$ and $(R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{2,3\},2)$. Therefore, the following capacity outer bound holds \begin{align} \left\{ \begin{array}{l} (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathbb{R}_+^3:\\ (R_1,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,3\},2)\\ (R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{2,3\},2)\\ (R_1,R_2)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2\},1) \end{array}\right\}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Swap (SIB5) for $(R_1,R_2)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2\},1)$, giving a simpler outer bound.
nodes.section: 4.2 Very strong interference from transmitter 3 to receiver 1

nodes.name: Receiver 1 can decode $X_3^n$ for free
nodes.statement: This outer bound can be achieved if we add one more condition on the PIMAC as we show next. If (\ref{VSI31-3}) holds then receiver 1 can decode $X_3^n$ while treating $X_1^n$ and $X_2^n$ as noise without imposing an additional rate constraint on $m_3$. This follows since (\ref{VSI31-3}) $\Rightarrow$ \begin{align} \frac{1}{2}\log\left(1+\frac{h_{31}^2P_3}{1+P_1+P_2}\right)\geq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_3). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Condition (VSI31-3) gives the rate inequality that lets receiver 1 decode $X_3^n$ as noise-limited.
nodes.section: 4.2 Very strong interference from transmitter 3 to receiver 1

nodes.name: Successive decoding at receiver 1 and MAC decoding at receiver 2
nodes.statement: Thus, receiver 1 can remove the contribution of $X_3^n$ from $Y_1^n$ and then decode $X_1^n$ and $X_2^n$ achieving $\mathcal{C}^M(\{1,2\},1)$. Let receiver 2 decode all signals in a MAC fashion achieving the region $(R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},2)$.
nodes.statement_short: Strip $X_3^n$ at receiver 1 to get $\mathcal{C}^M(\{1,2\},1)$; receiver 2 MAC-decodes all messages.
nodes.section: 4.2 Very strong interference from transmitter 3 to receiver 1

nodes.name: The extra power condition removes the sum-rate bound at receiver 2
nodes.statement: If we have \begin{align} h_{12}^2P_1+h_{22}^2P_2\geq(P_1+P_2)(1+P_3), \end{align} then the bound on $R_1+R_2+R_3$ in $\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},2)$ becomes redundant and can be removed. This follows since \begin{align} &h_{12}^2P_1+h_{22}^2P_2\geq(P_1+P_2)(1+P_3)\Rightarrow\\ &\frac{1}{2}\log(1+h_{12}^2P_1+h_{22}^2P_2+P_3)\geq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_1+P_2)\nonumber\\ &\hspace{5cm}+\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_3). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Under (VSI31-4) the three-user sum-rate constraint at receiver 2 is implied by the pairwise ones.
nodes.section: 4.2 Very strong interference from transmitter 3 to receiver 1

nodes.name: Conclude by region comparison
nodes.statement: Thus, under condition (\ref{VSI31-4}) and given $(R_1,R_2)\in\mathcal{C}^M(\{1,2\},1)$ we can replace $(R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2,3\},2)$ by \begin{align} (R_1,R_2)&\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2\},2)\\ (R_1,R_3)&\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,3\},2)\\ (R_2,R_3)&\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{2,3\},2). \end{align} Now, since the region $\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2\},2)$ is larger than $\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2\},1)$, we obtain the following theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Since $\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2\},2)$ contains $\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2\},1)$, the achievable region matches the outer bound.
nodes.section: 4.2 Very strong interference from transmitter 3 to receiver 1

nodes.name: Interference does not reduce capacity
nodes.statement: In this case, interference does not reduce capacity, i.e. the capacity region of the interference free MAC $M(\{1,2\},1)$ can be achieved by $(R_1,R_2)$ and the point-to-point capacity $R_3=\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_3)$ can also be achieved.
nodes.statement_short: State the target: interference-free MAC region plus full P2P rate.
nodes.section: 4.3 The PIMAC with very strong interference

nodes.name: Trivial outer bound
nodes.statement: Clearly, the following outer bound holds for the PIMAC \begin{align} \left\{ \begin{array}{l} (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathbb{R}_+^3:\\ R_3\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_3)\\ (R_1,R_2)\in\mathcal{C}_M(\{1,2\},1) \end{array}\right\}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: The interference-free P2P and MAC bounds are an outer bound.
nodes.section: 4.3 The PIMAC with very strong interference

nodes.name: Achievability by decoding interference first
nodes.statement: This outer bound can be achieved under the given conditions (\ref{pIMAC-VSI1}) and (\ref{pIMAC-VSI2}) by decoding interference first at each receiver while treating the desired signal as noise, and then decoding the desired signal after removing the contribution of interference. Thus, as if interference is not present, the capacity region of the pIMAC becomes as given in the following theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Each receiver decodes and removes the interference first, then its own signal.
nodes.section: 4.3 The PIMAC with very strong interference

nodes.name: Interference-free bounds on $R_3$ and $(R_1,R_2)$
nodes.statement: Clearly, for any achievable rate triple $(R_1,R_2,R_3)$, the rate $R_3$ is upper bounded by the interference free capacity of the P2P channel, and the rate couple $(R_1,R_2)$ is included in the capacity region of the interference free MAC $M(\{1,2\},1)$, i.e. \begin{align} R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_3)\\ (R_1,R_2)&\in\mathcal{C}^{M}(\{1,2\},1). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Removing interference can only help, giving the P2P and 2-user MAC bounds.

nodes.name: Genie gives $m_2$ to receiver 2 and yields a less noisy output
nodes.statement: Now we derive the other bounds. A genie gives $m_2$ as additional information to the second receiver. The obtained genie aided channel has a larger capacity region than the original PIMAC and can be used to outer bound $\mathcal{C}$. Now consider a rate tuple $(R_1,R_2,R_3)$ in the capacity region of the genie aided channel. This means that the first receiver and the second receiver are able to decode $(m_1,m_2)$ and $m_3$ reliably respectively. Since the second receiver is able to decode $m_3$, and since it knows $m_2$ from the genie, then it is able to construct \begin{align} \tilde{Y}_1^n&=\frac{Y_2^n-h_{22}X_2^n-X_3^n}{h_{12}}+X_2^n+h_{31}X_3^n\nonumber\\ &=X_1^n+X_2^n+h_{31}X_3^n+\frac{1}{h_{12}}Z_2^n \end{align} If $h_{12}^2\geq1$, then $\tilde{Y}_1^n$ is a less noisy version of $Y_1^n$. So if the first receiver is able to decode $m_1$ then so does the second receiver. Thus $(R_1,R_3)$ is contained in the MAC region of $M(\{2,3\},2)$, i.e. \begin{align} (R_1,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}^{M}(\{1,3\},2) \text{ if } h_{12}^2\geq1. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: With $m_2$ known, receiver 2 reconstructs $\tilde{Y}_1^n$, less noisy than $Y_1^n$ when $h_{12}^2\geq1$.

nodes.name: Symmetric bound for $(R_2,R_3)$
nodes.statement: Similarly, we can show that \begin{align} (R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}^{M}(\{2,3\},2) &\text{ if } h_{22}^2\geq1. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: The same genie argument with roles swapped gives the $(R_2,R_3)$ MAC bound.

nodes.name: Bound from receiver 1 decoding all three messages
nodes.statement: Finally, for any rate triple $(R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}$, the first receiver is able to decode $m_1$ and $m_2$ reliably. Thus, if $h_{31}^2\geq1$, receiver 1 can construct a less noisy version of $Y_2^n$ and then decode $m_3$ reliably leading to the bound \begin{align} (R_1,R_2,R_3)\in\mathcal{C}^{M}(\{1,2,3\},1) &\text{ if } h_{31}^2\geq1. \end{align} and the statement of the Lemma is proved.
nodes.statement_short: If $h_{31}^2\geq1$ receiver 1 can also decode $m_3$, giving the three-user MAC bound.

nodes.name: Expand the inner bound into explicit rate constraints
nodes.statement: We can expand the achievable region $\underline{\mathcal{C}}$ to obtain the following rate constraints for the achievable region \begin{align*} R_1&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_1,h_{12}^2P_1\})\\ R_2&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_2,h_{22}^2P_2\})\\ R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_3,h_{31}^2P_3\})\\ R_1+R_2&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_1+P_2,h_{12}^2P_1+h_{22}^2P_2\})\\ R_1+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_1+h_{31}^2P_3,h_{12}^2P_1+P_3\})\\ R_2+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_2+h_{31}^2P_3,h_{22}^2P_2+P_3\})\\ R_1+R_2+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+\min\{P_1+P_2+h_{31}^2P_3,\\ &\hspace{3cm}h_{12}^2P_1+h_{22}^2P_2+P_3\}) \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Write the intersection of the two MAC regions as seven min-form rate constraints.

nodes.name: Simplify the constraints under the strong interference conditions
nodes.statement: Using conditions (\ref{pSI1}) and (\ref{pSI2}), these constraints reduce to \begin{align*} R_i&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_i),\ \forall i\in\{1,2,3\}\\ R_1+R_2&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_1+P_2)\\ R_1+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_1+h_{31}^2P_3)\\ R_1+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+h_{12}^2P_1+P_3)\\ R_2+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_2+h_{31}^2P_3)\\ R_2+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+h_{22}^2P_2+P_3)\\ R_1+R_2+R_3&\leq\frac{1}{2}\log(1+P_1+P_2+h_{31}^2P_3). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Substituting the two conditions resolves every minimum, collapsing the list.

nodes.name: Match the expansion of the outer bound
nodes.statement: Expanding $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$ when conditions (\ref{pSI1}) and (\ref{pSI2}) hold lead to the same rate constraints. Thus, the two regions $\overline{\mathcal{C}}$ and $\underline{\mathcal{C}}$ coincide and the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: The outer bound expands to the same constraint list, so the two regions coincide.

nodes.name: Define the genie signals
nodes.statement: Consider the following signals \begin{align} S_1^n&=h_{12}X_1^n+h_{22}X_2^n+\eta_1W_1^n\\ S_2^n&=h_{31}X_3^n+\eta_2W_2^n \end{align} where $\eta_i\in\mathbb{R}$ and $W_i^n$ is an i.i.d. sequence with $W_i\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ for $i\in\{1,2\}$ such that $\mathbb{E}[W_iZ_i]=\rho_i$. A genie gives these signals as extra information to the receivers. Thus, receiver $i$ knows both $Y_i^n$ and $S_i^n$ and uses them for decoding.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $S_1^n,S_2^n$ with noise correlated to $Z_i$ and hand them to the receivers.

nodes.name: Apply Fano's inequality
nodes.statement: Using Fano's inequality, we have \begin{align} n(R_1+R_2)&\leq I(X_1^n,X_2^n;Y_1^n,S_1^n)+n\epsilon_{1n}\\ nR_3&\leq I(X_3^n;Y_2^n,S_2^n)+n\epsilon_{2n} \end{align} where $\epsilon_{1n},\epsilon_{2n}\to0$ as $n\to\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Fano bounds $n(R_1+R_2)$ and $nR_3$ by the genie-aided mutual informations.

nodes.name: Chain rule expansion into differential entropies
nodes.statement:
Using the chain rule, we can write  egin{align} n(R_1+R_2-\epsilon_{1n})&\leq I(X_1^n,X_2^n;S_1^n)+I(X_1^n,X_2^n;Y_1^n|S_1^n)
onumber\ &=h(S_1^n)-h(S_1^n|X_1^n,X_2^n)+h(Y_1^n|S_1^n)
onumber\ &\quad-h(Y_1^n|S_1^n,X_1^n,X_2^n). \end{align} Similarly  egin{align} n(R_3-\epsilon_{2n})&\leq h(S_2^n)-h(S_2^n|X_3^n)+h(Y_2^n|S_2^n)
onumber\ &\quad-h(Y_2^n|S_2^n,X_3^n). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Expand both mutual informations into four differential entropy terms each.

nodes.name: Gaussian maximization of the conditional entropies
nodes.statement: The next step is to show that sum of the above quantities (\ref{Q1}) and (\ref{Q2}) are maximized when $X_i^n$ is i.i.d. Gaussian for all $i\in\{1,2,3\}$, i.e. $X_i\sim\mathcal{N}(0,P_i^*)$ where $P_i^*\leq P_i$. We will denote that Gaussian $X_i$ as $X_{iG}$ and the corresponding outputs as $Y_{iG}$ and $S_{iG}$. Since the Gaussian distribution maximizes the conditional differential entropy under a covariance constraint, we have \begin{align} h(Y_1^n|S_1^n)&\leq nh(Y_{1G}|S_{1G})\\ h(Y_2^n|S_2^n)&\leq nh(Y_{2G}|S_{2G}). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Gaussian inputs maximize the conditional differential entropy under a covariance constraint.

nodes.name: Jointly maximize the entropy difference via worst-case noise
nodes.statement:
Furthermore, the terms $h(S_1^n|X_1^n,X_2^n)$ and $h(S_2^n|X_3^n)$ are independent of the distribution of $X_i$. Now, we jointly maximize the difference $h(S_1^n)-h(Y_2^n|S_2^n,X_3^n)$ as follows  egin{align} &\hspace{-1cm}h(S_1^n)-h(Y_2^n|S_2^n,X_3^n)
onumber\ &=h(h_{12}X_1^n+h_{22}X_2^n+\eta_1W_1^n)
onumber\ &\quad-h(h_{12}X_1^n+h_{22}X_2^n+Z_2^n|W_2^n)\ &\stackrel{(a)}{=}h(h_{12}X_1^n+h_{22}X_2^n+\eta_1W_1^n)
onumber\ &\quad-h(h_{12}X_1^n+h_{22}X_2^n+V_2^n)\ &\stackrel{(b)}{\leq}nh(h_{12}X_{1G}+h_{22}X_{2G}+\eta_1W_1)
onumber\ &\quad-nh(h_{12}X_{1G}+h_{22}X_{2G}+V_2)\ &=nh(S_{1G})-nh(Y_{2G}|S_{2G},X_{3G},X_{4G}), \end{align} where $(a)$ follows from \cite[Lemma 6]{AnnapureddyVeeravalli} with $V_2^n$ being an i.i.d. Gaussian sequence with $V_2\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1-ho_2^2)$ and $(b)$ from the worst case noise \cite{DiggaviCover} such that $\eta_1^2\leq 1-ho_2^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Use the cited Lemma 6 and the worst-case-noise result to bound the entropy difference by its Gaussian value.

nodes.name: Monotonicity in the powers and conclusion
nodes.statement: Since $\eta_1^2\leq1-\rho_2^2$, (\ref{T1}) can be shown to be increasing in $P_1^*$ and $P_2^*$ and thus is maximized by $X_{iG}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,P_i)$. Similarly, if $\eta_2^2\leq1-\rho_1^2$, $h(S_2^n)-h(Y_1^n|S_1^n,X_1^n,X_2^n)$ can be shown to be maximized by $X_{iG}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,P_i)$. Moreover, $h(Y_{1G}|S_{1G})$ and $h(Y_{2G}|S_{2G})$ can be shown to be increasing in $P_i^*$ and thus also maximized by $X_{iG}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,P_i)$. As a result, by letting $n\to\infty$ \begin{align} &R_1+R_2+R_3\nonumber\\ &\quad\leq I(X_{1G},X_{2G};Y_{1G},S_{1G})+I(X_{3G};Y_{2G},S_{2G}) \end{align} with $X_{iG}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,P_i)$ and $\eta_i\leq1-\rho_j^2$.
nodes.statement_short: All terms increase in $P_i^*$, so full power $X_{iG}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,P_i)$ maximizes and the sum-rate bound follows.
